newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Prodi upbeat on Italy's EMU prospects.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Prodi upbeat on Italy's EMU prospects.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi expressed renewed optimism on Wednesday that Italy would trim its 1997 budget deficit by enough to join Europe's planned single currency from the start.

The centre-left leader made his assessment in parliament, where he faced opposition charges of deceiving Italians into thinking the country had a chance of making the starting line-up for economic and monetary union (EMU).

Reporting back on talks last week with Chancellor Helmut Kohl of Germany, Prodi told the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) that Italy already met key conditions on interest rates, inflation and exchange rates.
"We will meet the ratio between deficit and GDP in the terms laid down by Maastricht," Prodi added.
The Maastricht Treaty requires countries to keep their 1997 deficit within three percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in order to join EMU from its planned January 1, 1999 start date.
Prodi said Italy was also moving towards the final Maastricht goal of debt approaching 60 percent of GDP. Italy is aiming for a debt-GDP ratio of 120.6 percent for 1997.
"The credibility of the government's action is fully appreciated by our European partners," Prodi said.
"They all believe that the Italian strategy is the most vigorous and most appropriate for entering EMU," he said.

A Reuters survey of 32 economists published on Wednesday showed Italy was on course to fulfil as many of the rules as Germany for entry into the single currency, the euro, but that both looked like failing on the size of their deficit and debt ratios.
Analysts said Rome's entry would probably have to be delayed because of the weight of German public opinion against a euro which includes the lira from the start.

"Chancellor Kohl has to sell the single currency to the German people. To do that Italy would have to be excluded for a couple of years," said one contributor to the poll, which was conducted between February 5 and 10.

Prodi's insistence that Italy stood a strong chance drew jeers from opposition benches in parliament, where one centre-right politician, Marco Taradash, accused the prime minister of "tricking" Italians.
His criticism was echoed outside the Chamber by hard-right leader Gianfranco Fini, who told foreign journalists that Prodi should honour a pledge to quit if Italy fails to make EMU by resigning now.
Fini said Prodi was adopting "accounting tricks and special taxes" to lower Italy's 1997 deficit and doubted whether the ratio could be sustained without structural cuts to spending.
Italy has drawn up a 62.5 trillion lire ($38 billion) austerity budget for 1997 that includes an unpopular one-off "Euro tax" to help cut the deficit.

Prodi has said future budgets must tackle welfare spending and the costly pensions system, but faces stiff resistance from the hard left party Communist Refoundation, which assures the coalition government's majority in parliament.
The main opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance has offered to support an early budget for 1998 if it tackles reform of the welfare state.

Freedom Alliance leader Silvio Berlusconi alleged on Wednesday that the government was now backing away from an early budget, initially proposed by Prodi to signal Italy's commitment to serious reform of its state finances.
